Live production compared

vMix vs ATEM: a Windows switcher or a Blackmagic box?

By Syd Lawrence, a visual artist and developer who makes Vibresia. Facts last checked 2 November 2026; updated 3 November 2026.

If you are running a multi-camera show on a Windows PC and want switching, recording and streaming in one application, pick vMix: the one-off licence starts at US$60 and the same features on a subscription are US$50 a month. If you would rather the switching happened inside a box of its own and you want the control panel to run on your Mac, pick ATEM, where the ATEM Mini Pro is US$445 and the control software is free. The fact that settles most of these comparisons is the platform, because vMix has no macOS build, while ATEM Software Control runs on Mac and Windows but does nothing until a switcher is connected to it.

These are live-show tools. vMix and ATEM run a show: they send video to a projector, a mixer or a capture card. Vibresia, which we make, is not one of those. It has no MIDI, OSC, NDI or Syphon output, no timeline and no projection mapping — its only job is music in and picture out, on the Mac you are sitting at.

If you are after a visual for whatever your Mac is playing, Vibresia is the free app that does that. If you are setting up a show, this page is the right one.

Every row comes from the app's own documentation, on the date shown in the sources below. "Not that we could find" means we could not find it documented, not that the app cannot do it.

Pick vMix if

you are running a multi-camera production on a Windows PC and want switching, recording, streaming and instant replay in one application. Basic HD is US$60 once, and the full edition is US$50 a month, with a 60-day trial of the Pro edition to try it on.

Pick ATEM if

you want the switching done in hardware so the show does not depend on how fast your computer is, and you want the control panel to run on a Mac as well as on Windows. The ATEM Mini Pro is US$445 and ATEM Software Control is free to install on unlimited computers, but the switcher is the purchase.

Why people compare them

They come up together because they are being asked to do the same job: several cameras, one programme output, and a recording and a stream at the end of it. vMix is a live video production and streaming switcher for Windows that mixes cameras, network sources and media, then records and streams the result. ATEM is Live production switchers for cutting, keying, mixing and streaming multiple video sources, with a free control panel for Mac and Windows.

Underneath that they are not the same kind of thing. vMix is an application you install on a Windows PC, and the computer does the switching. ATEM is a box that does the switching itself, with a control panel on your screen that has to be plugged into that box before it will do anything at all.

The difference decides the price too. A vMix licence starts at US$60 for software you run on a machine you already own. The cheapest ATEM switcher is US$445 of hardware, and the family runs up to US$10,515. So the question behind most of these comparisons is whether the show needs a computer doing the work, or a box doing the work and a computer only pointing at it.

Both are production tools rather than performers. You set up your sources, choose where the output goes, and then let it run.

Where vMix wins

It does the whole job on one machine you already own. Mixes cameras, capture cards, NDI, OMT and SRT sources with transitions, overlays and titles, and records and streams the same production at the same time

It gets the picture to other machines over NDI. Sends program output to other machines over NDI, with up to four independently configurable NDI outputs in the 4K, Pro and Max editions

It has remote guests and instant replay. Handles remote guests with vMix Call for up to eight callers, and slow-motion instant replay for up to eight cameras

It can be driven from the desk. vMix accepts MIDI from controllers for shortcuts, and can send MIDI out to lights and faders through its Activators feature. Can be scripted, driven from a web controller, or controlled from MIDI devices and PTZ cameras from the 4K edition upwards

The trial runs the paid edition. The trial lasts 60 days and runs vMix Pro with all its features, including 4K, MultiCorder and full Instant Replay. A paid licence is needed after the 60 days.

It costs less to begin with. The cheapest edition, Basic HD at 60 dollars, is limited to four total inputs, three of them cameras or NDI, 1920 by 1080 output and one overlay channel, and it leaves out vMix Call, MultiCorder, Instant Replay, scripting, PTZ control, the Mix input and the extra outputs.

Where ATEM wins

The video work happens in the hardware. The video work happens in the hardware, so the switcher streams from its own engine and does not depend on a fast computer.

The control panel is free and can go on every computer. The free ATEM Software Control can be installed on unlimited computers, so several people can work on one show at the same time.

The ISO models record every input separately. The ISO models record every input to separate files with matching timecode and save a DaVinci Resolve project file for editing.

There are no licence fees on the switcher features. Program and preview switching, DVEs, SuperSource, chroma keyers and the Fairlight mixer are all included with no licence fees or monthly charges.

The picture leaves the box in broadcast shapes. Program video leaves the switcher over HDMI, SDI and a USB webcam connection, so it feeds projectors, recorders, Zoom and streaming software.

It runs on a Mac as well as on Windows. ATEM Software Control is listed for Mac and Windows. ATEM Software Control is built for macOS and Windows only, so there is no Linux version.

Where both fall short

The Mac answer is not the same on each side. There is no macOS version of vMix, as it cannot be installed directly on OSX and can only be installed on Windows via Boot Camp on older Intel Macs. ATEM Software Control cannot be used on its own, because the software control panel must be connected to a switcher to run.

Their video over IP does not meet. vMix receives NDI sources from the network and sends its output over NDI, with up to four independently configurable NDI outputs in the 4K, Pro and Max editions. ATEM takes video over IP as RTMP or SRT streams from Blackmagic cameras, and NDI is not a supported input or output.

Their MIDI is different too. vMix accepts MIDI from controllers for shortcuts, and can send MIDI out to lights and faders through its Activators feature. ATEM Software Control reads MIDI, with a MIDI controller mapped to switcher buttons and Mackie Control surfaces driving the audio mixer faders. The ATEM manual describes no MIDI output to other applications.

Neither documents OSC, Syphon or Spout. The vMix guide gives OSC and Spout as not that we could find, and it states that vMix has no Syphon input or output, because there is no macOS version of vMix, and Mac sources reach vMix through NDI or OMT scan converters instead. The ATEM Mini Manual and the ATEM Television Studio Manual do not mention OSC, Syphon or Spout either.

The ATEM Mini line is HD only. The ATEM Mini line is HD only, since Blackmagic lists no Ultra HD video standards for these switchers.

Neither one is a music visualiser. Both are general tools for video, and both expect you to bring the content and the cues with you.

What it costs

vMix charges in US dollars. The one-off licences are Basic HD at US$60, HD at US$350, 4K at US$700 and Pro at US$1,200, each one including twelve months of free version updates. The subscription edition, vMix Max, is US$50 a month and carries the same features as Pro, with free version updates while it is paid for.

The ATEM family is priced per box, not per seat. The ATEM Mini Pro is US$445, the ATEM Mini Extreme ISO G2 is US$3,479, the ATEM Television Studio HD8 is US$2,965, the ATEM Television Studio 4K8 is US$6,445 and the ATEM 4 M/E Constellation 4K is US$10,515. The listed prices are the US MSRP in dollars and include duties but exclude sales tax and shipping.

ATEM Software Control cannot be used on its own, because the software control panel must be connected to a switcher to run. ATEM Software Control is free and may be run on unlimited computers, but it controls hardware and does not include a switcher, so the family as a whole has no free tier.

Questions people ask

Can I use the free ATEM Software Control without the switcher?

No. ATEM Software Control cannot be used on its own, because the software control panel must be connected to a switcher to run. ATEM Software Control is free to download and can be run on unlimited computers, but it controls hardware rather than making a show of its own.

Which one is cheaper, vMix or ATEM?

vMix is the cheaper place to start. Its one-off licence begins at US$60 and the subscription is US$50 a month. The cheapest ATEM box is the ATEM Mini Pro at US$445, and the family runs up to US$10,515.

Does vMix run on a Mac?

No. There is no macOS version of vMix, as it cannot be installed directly on OSX and can only be installed on Windows via Boot Camp on older Intel Macs. ATEM Software Control runs on Mac and Windows, so on a Mac the ATEM is the one of the two that works on your own hardware, as long as a switcher is connected to it.

Can I try either of them before I buy?

vMix, yes. The trial lasts 60 days and runs vMix Pro with all its features, including 4K, MultiCorder and full Instant Replay. A paid licence is needed after the 60 days. The ATEM family has no free tier, because the control panel needs the switcher to run.
